claims.text: Service-regime thermal exposure causes the metastable solid-solution matrix in Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys to decompose into intermetallic precipitates.
The decomposition of the metastable matrix is kinetically driven.
A processing route that produces a more inhomogeneous thermal history accelerates intermetallic formation.
A more inhomogeneous thermal history produces microsegregation of Mg and other alloying elements.
A more uniform processing route helps retain the metastable solid-solution chemistry.
Retention of the solid-solution chemistry supports high-temperature oxidation resistance.
Retention of the solid-solution chemistry supports corrosion resistance.
Differences in processing-route thermal history create different degrees of compositional inhomogeneity.
Differences in processing-route thermal history create different degrees of residual stress.
Compositional inhomogeneity and residual stresses drive the nucleation and growth of intermetallic phases.
Intermetallic phases nucleate preferentially at sites of Mg segregation.
Intermetallic phases disrupt the initially homogeneous, corrosion-resistant matrix.
A more uniform processing route delays or minimizes intermetallic precipitation.
Specimens produced with greater thermal gradients will form intermetallic compounds faster during aging than specimens produced with minimized thermal inhomogeneity.
Specimens produced with greater thermal gradients will exhibit marked Mg segregation.
Greater intermetallic formation and Mg segregation will correlate with degraded high-temperature oxidation resistance relative to the initial metastable state.
Greater intermetallic formation and Mg segregation will correlate with degraded corrosion resistance relative to the initial metastable state.
Greater intermetallic formation and Mg segregation will correlate with worse oxidation and corrosion performance than in specimens made by a more thermally homogeneous route.
Diffusion-driven precipitation becomes relevant after sufficient exposure time near the onset of oxidation-induced degradation.
